planting.note: Direct sow from 4 weeks before the last frost through late spring, then resume in late summer for a fall crop; roots hold in the ground and keep their texture longer than fast round red radishes, making this a useful bridge variety between spring and autumn plantings.

directions: Sow seed 1/2 inch deep directly in the garden and thin seedlings to 2-3 inches apart once true leaves appear. Violet de Gournay is a French market-garden heirloom named for the Normandy town of Gournay, producing round to slightly oval roots with smooth deep violet-black skin surrounding crisp white flesh. It matures faster than the larger Black Spanish winter radishes it is sometimes confused with, and its flavor is notably milder, making it suited to fresh eating rather than storage. Keep soil evenly moist during root sizing to prevent the skin from cracking or turning woody.
sources: Kokopelli Seed Foundation heirloom radish collection

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring and succession sow every 2 weeks until temperatures climb; the compact foliage tolerates closer spacing than most spring radishes, allowing more roots per row-foot.

directions: Broadcast or row-sow 1/2 inch deep and thin to about 1 inch apart, since the short, upright tops leave little room for foliage to compete for light. Long Scarlet Short Top is a nineteenth-century market variety producing tapered, cylindrical scarlet roots 5-6 inches long, distinguished from other 'long scarlet' types by its notably reduced leaf growth, which was bred deliberately to permit tighter row spacing for commercial growers. Pull roots promptly once they reach usable size, as the slender shape can turn pithy and hollow faster than round varieties if left in warm soil. The tapered form and quick maturity made it a standard early-spring forcing radish before greenhouse culture became common.
sources: W. Atlee Burpee & Co. historical seed catalog archives

planting.note: Direct sow 8-10 weeks before the first fall frost so roots size up in cooling weather; unlike spring radishes, Celestial is grown specifically as a fall/winter storage crop and bolts readily if sown in spring heat.

directions: Sow seed 1/2 inch deep into deeply worked soil and thin early to prevent forked roots, since mature roots can reach 6-8 inches long and 2-3 inches thick. Celestial, also sold as China White, is a large all-white winter radish predating most modern daikon strains in Western seed trade, producing dense, crisp flesh that stores well in a root cellar or in the ground under mulch through early winter. Its flavor is milder and sweeter than black winter radishes but firmer and more substantial than spring salad types, making it well suited to braising, roasting, and long-keeping pickles. Harvest after a light frost for the best texture and flavor concentration.

planting.note: Direct sow 6-10 weeks before the first fall frost for the sweetest roots, or in very early spring for a quicker, less reliable spring crop; the upright strap leaves stay cleaner than cut-leaf types, making them easier to harvest for greens without soil-splashed foliage.

directions: Direct sow 1/4 inch deep in rows and thin to 4-6 inches, using thinnings as tender greens. Purple Top Strap Leaf is a nineteenth-century dual-purpose heirloom distinguished from ordinary purple-top turnips by its smooth, non-lobed 'strap' leaves, which grow upright rather than sprawling and stay cleaner in wet weather, making them a preferred choice for market growers selling bunched turnip greens alongside the roots. The flattened globe roots are white below the soil line with a purple-red crown above, mild-flavored when harvested young. This foliage trait, rather than root shape or color, is what sets it apart from other purple-top selections still common in seed catalogs.

planting.note: Direct sow 8-10 weeks before the first fall frost into loose, deeply worked soil so the tapered root can push freely; a spring sowing is possible but the root tends toward more pungent flavor and faster bolting in warming soil.

directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep and thin to 4-6 inches apart; because much of the root pushes up out of the soil as it grows, mounding a little loose soil around the shoulders keeps the exposed portion from toughening or turning green. Long White Cow Horn is an early American heirloom named for its distinctive shape: a slender, curved, carrot-like white root that tapers to a point, growing half-exposed above ground rather than forming a globe. It matures faster than round white-fleshed turnips and was traditionally valued for both table use when young and livestock feed when left to size up. The exposed shoulders develop a slight green blush in sunlight, which does not affect the mild flavor of the flesh beneath.
sources: Sturtevant's Notes on Edible Plants (U.P. Hedrick, ed.)

planting.note: Direct sow 8-10 weeks before the first fall frost in lean, sandy soil; unlike most turnips, Teltow develops its characteristic concentrated flavor best when grown lean rather than in rich, heavily amended beds.

directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in rows and thin to 2-3 inches apart, since this variety forms small, slender, finger-sized roots rather than a large globe. Teltow Turnip is a German heirloom from the sandy soils around Teltow near Berlin, historically prized enough that it was reportedly shipped to Weimar for Goethe's table, and it remains catalogued in European heirloom seed-saving collections today. The roots are pale yellowish-white with a dense, waxy texture and an intense, nutty flavor unlike the milder taste of larger globe turnips, traditionally used in slow-simmered stews rather than eaten raw. Growing it in poor, sandy ground rather than rich garden soil is essential to concentrating its distinctive flavor.
sources: Slow Food International, Ark of Taste catalog
Kokopelli Seed Foundation heirloom vegetable collection

planting.note: Direct sow from 4 weeks before the last frost into late spring, and again in late summer for fall harvest; being a fast, small-rooted type it is well suited to tight succession sowing every 10-14 days.

directions: Sow 1/2 inch deep and thin to about 1-2 inches apart; harvest promptly once roots reach 1 inch across, as the globe shape turns pithy faster than elongated types if left in the ground. Scarlet Turnip White Tipped is an old French and American market-garden heirloom distinguished by its round, turnip-like shape rather than the oblong 'half-long' form of French Breakfast, with bright scarlet skin fading to white at the root tip. It was cultivated as a distinct forcing and early-market variety well before French Breakfast rose to prominence, and the two were listed as separate cultivars in nineteenth-century French seed catalogs. Its crisp texture and mild bite make it a good choice for growers wanting a quick round radish with more color contrast than solid-red types.
